planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light in a chunky, well-drained aroid mix; give the climbing stems a moss pole or bark slab to attach to as they mature, since leaf size and texture improve with vertical support.

directions: This hybrid trade cultivar produces heavily quilted, mottled light green and cream leaves with a dimpled, almost reptilian surface texture reminiscent of the collector species Philodendron verrucosum, though it is considerably easier to grow and tolerates average home humidity better than true verrucosum. Young plants stay compact and bushy, then begin to climb once a few mature leaves have formed, so provide a moss pole or let it trail from a shelf. Keep it in bright, indirect light to hold the leaf contrast, since deep shade causes the foliage to green up and lose definition. Allow the top inch or two of potting mix to dry between waterings and avoid cold drafts below 55°F.
sources: International Aroid Society reference
commercial grower cultivation notes (Costa Farms, specialty aroid retailers)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light in well-drained, chunky potting mix; provide a moss pole for the climbing stems and keep humidity above 50% to encourage full-sized, well-variegated leaves.

directions: A variegated sport of the classic climbing cultivar 'Red Emerald,' this selection carries dark reddish stems and petioles beneath leaves splashed in shifting patterns of cream, pink, and green, with some leaves emerging almost entirely pink before mellowing. Bright, indirect light is important for sustaining the pink and cream sectors, since low light pushes new growth back toward plain green. Train it onto a moss pole as it climbs, and remove any all-white or chlorophyll-free leaves that cannot support themselves, which helps the plant stay vigorous. Let the mix dry slightly between waterings and avoid letting temperatures drop below 55°F.
sources: International Aroid Society reference
commercial grower cultivation notes (Gabriella Plants, specialty aroid retailers)

planting.note: Divide rooted basal offsets or plant container-grown specimens in rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; this self-heading dwarf stays far smaller than straight species selloum and fits well in pots or small garden beds.

directions: Super Atom is a dwarf, non-climbing selection of the common tree philodendron, forming a dense, low rosette of deeply lobed, ruffled, glossy dark green leaves at roughly a quarter the mature size of plain selloum. Because it stays compact and never develops a visible trunk, it works well as a houseplant specimen, a patio container plant, or a shaded foundation planting where full-sized selloum would quickly overwhelm the space. Grow in bright, filtered light to keep the leaf lobing tight and well defined, since deep shade produces larger, more open leaves and a looser habit. It tolerates brief light frost in zone 9 once established, resprouting from the crown, and otherwise wants the same consistently moist, well-drained soil as other aroids.
sources: commercial grower cultivation notes (Top Tropicals, specialty aroid retailers)
International Aroid Society reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or terrarium specimen in a wide, shallow container that accommodates the creeping rhizome; keep the rhizome at the soil surface and provide high humidity (60%+) and warmth, since this Sumatran species is less tolerant of dry indoor air than many rhizomatous begonias.

directions: Native to the humid forests of Sumatra, Begonia goegoensis forms a low rhizomatous mound of rounded, quilted leaves in deep bronze-green with a fine, spiderweb-like network of pale silvery veins radiating across the surface, giving the foliage an almost smoldering, fire-lit appearance in low light. It grows best in warm, consistently humid conditions, making it a natural fit for enclosed terrariums, greenhouses, or humidity domes rather than open, dry rooms. Keep it out of direct sun, which bleaches the rich leaf color, and let the rhizome creep across the soil surface rather than burying it. Propagate by dividing rooted rhizome sections, each with at least one growth point.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Begonia goegoensis profile
American Begonia Society — rhizomatous begonia species notes

planting.note: Grow in a wide, shallow pot that allows the creeping rhizome room to spread; keep the rhizome at the soil surface and let the top inch of mix dry between waterings to avoid rot.

directions: Begonia conchifolia is a Central American rhizomatous species named for its thick, fleshy, concave leaves that curl slightly at the edges like a shell or clamshell, typically a glossy mid-green sometimes marked with darker spotting. It is the parent species behind several popular compact rhizomatous hybrids sold under 'Tiger' trade names, though the straight species itself is less commonly offered and worth seeking out for its simpler, waxier leaf form. Grow in bright indirect light with moderate humidity, allowing the rhizome to creep across the soil surface rather than burying it. Propagate readily from leaf or rhizome cuttings.
sources: American Begonia Society — rhizomatous begonia species notes
Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder

planting.note: Grow in a wide, shallow pot in bright indirect light; keep the rhizome at the soil surface and allow the top inch of mix to dry between waterings.

directions: Introduced by Logee's Greenhouses as an exclusive hybrid, this rhizomatous begonia was selected during a visit by its namesake for its deeply spiraled leaves in soft tones of tan, chartreuse, and bronze, edged with fine chocolate-brown markings along the margins. It forms a compact, mounding clump that stays well under a foot tall, making it a good fit for windowsills and small containers. Sprays of small pale pink flowers appear above the foliage in winter, adding seasonal interest to what is primarily a foliage plant. Grow in bright indirect light with moderate humidity and propagate by dividing the creeping rhizome.
sources: Logee's Greenhouses — Begonia 'Martha Stewart' introduction notes
American Begonia Society — rhizomatous begonia hybrid notes

planting.note: Grow in a shallow pot or terrarium in bright indirect light; this miniature rhizomatous hybrid stays small and is well suited to windowsill and terrarium culture.

directions: Tiger Kitten is a compact rhizomatous begonia hybrid with small, rounded, chocolate-green leaves overlaid with irregular golden-yellow spotting, forming a dense, mounding clump that rarely exceeds a few inches tall. Its diminutive scale and neat habit make it a popular choice for terrariums, dish gardens, and other small enclosed displays where larger rhizomatous begonias would quickly outgrow the space. Grow in bright, indirect light with consistently high humidity, since shriveling leaf edges usually signal air that is too dry. Allow the soil surface to dry slightly between waterings and propagate by dividing the rhizome.
sources: commercial grower listings (Harmony Foliage, specialty begonia retailers)
American Begonia Society — rhizomatous begonia hybrid notes

planting.note: Grow in a wide, shallow pot in bright indirect light; this dark-leaved rhizomatous hybrid holds its deepest color with consistent humidity and protection from direct sun.

directions: Night Eyes is a modern rhizomatous begonia hybrid bred for near-black, dark purple foliage that reads almost charcoal in low light and takes on warmer plum tones under brighter conditions. Like other dark-leaved rhizomatous begonias, it benefits from bright indirect light to keep the coloration deep and saturated, since too little light tends to green the foliage and too much direct sun can scorch it. Grow it in a shallow container that lets the creeping rhizome spread across the soil surface, and allow the top inch of mix to dry between waterings to prevent rot. Propagate by dividing rooted rhizome sections.
sources: commercial grower listings (Harmony Foliage)
American Begonia Society — rhizomatous begonia hybrid notes

planting.note: Grow year-round indoors in bright indirect light, or move pots to a sheltered, shaded outdoor spot once nights stay reliably above 50°F.

directions: This sport of the long-cultivated Beefsteak Begonia ('Begonia erythrophylla') is distinguished by a tight spiral or helix twist where each glossy, rounded leaf meets its petiole, adding a sculptural quality to foliage that is otherwise identical to the parent plant: olive-green above with a deep red reverse and a fine fringe of red hairs along the margin. Grow in bright, indirect light, since it tolerates somewhat lower light than many rhizomatous begonias but holds its leaf color and curl best with some gentle morning sun. Let the soil surface dry between waterings to protect the thick creeping rhizome from rot, and maintain moderate to high humidity for steady growth. Propagate by rhizome division or leaf-petiole cuttings.
sources: commercial grower listings (Steve's Leaves, specialty begonia retailers)
American Begonia Society — rhizomatous begonia variety notes

planting.note: Grow in a small pot or terrarium in bright indirect light with very high humidity (60%+); this West African hybrid is best suited to enclosed terrariums or greenhouse conditions rather than open dry rooms.

directions: Buttercup is a small, shrubby begonia hybrid between two West African species, Begonia microsperma and Begonia prismatocarpa, producing rounded, smooth, bright chartreuse-green leaves and cheerful bright yellow flowers that bloom nearly continuously under good conditions. Its diminutive size and near-constant flowering make it a favorite for terrariums and vivariums, where the enclosed humidity suits it far better than an open, dry windowsill. Keep it out of direct sun, which can scorch the thin leaves, and maintain consistently moist (not soggy) soil and high ambient humidity. Propagate easily from stem cuttings rooted in moist medium.
sources: commercial grower listings (Glass Box Tropicals, Black Jungle Terrarium Supply)
American Begonia Society — species hybrid notes

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in warm, moist medium; grow in bright, indirect light in well-drained potting mix and let the soil dry between waterings, since this semi-succulent species stores moisture in its fleshy leaves and stems.

directions: Native to tropical South America, Peperomia pereskiifolia produces narrow, fleshy, deep green leaves arranged in distinctive whorls of three to four around reddish stems, giving the plant a layered, almost pagoda-like silhouette. It stays compact and upright, making it a good choice for shelves and windowsills where a smaller footprint is useful. Grow in bright, indirect light, which keeps growth dense; lower light causes the whorled leaf spacing to stretch and loosen. Allow the potting mix to dry between waterings, since like most peperomias it is more prone to root rot from overwatering than from occasional neglect.
sources: commercial grower listings (Steve's Leaves, specialty houseplant retailers)
Royal Horticultural Society — Peperomia cultivation

planting.note: Root stem or leaf cuttings in warm, barely moist medium; grow in bright, indirect light in very well-drained, slightly gritty potting mix and let the soil dry out fully between waterings.

directions: Peperomia axillaris earns its 'taco' nickname from its small, thick, boat-shaped leaves that fold gently upward along the midrib, green on the upper surface and tinged burgundy underneath. It forms a dense, shrubby, mounding clump on woody stems and grows slowly, staying well suited to small pots and tabletop displays. As a semi-succulent species it is more sensitive to overwatering than to drought, so use a fast-draining, gritty mix and let it dry out completely between waterings. Bright, indirect light keeps the compact, bushy habit tight; low light causes leggy, stretched growth.
sources: commercial grower listings (Sprout Home, Planet Desert, specialty houseplant retailers)
Royal Horticultural Society — Peperomia cultivation

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in moist, humus-rich soil in bright indirect shade; variegated arrowroot grows taller and more upright than the familiar prayer plant (Maranta leuconeura) and benefits from consistent moisture and high humidity.

directions: This variegated selection of arrowroot, the same species historically grown as a tropical starch crop, produces broad, lance-shaped leaves marbled in cream and white over green, carried on taller, more upright stems than the low-growing prayer plant most houseplant growers know. It lacks the pronounced nyctinastic leaf-folding of Maranta leuconeura, but shares its preference for consistently moist, humus-rich soil, high humidity, and bright, indirect shade protected from direct sun, which scorches the pale variegated tissue. Divide the spreading rhizome to propagate, and mulch or mist regularly to keep humidity elevated around the foliage. Outdoors in frost-free zones it forms an attractive clumping groundcover in shaded beds.
sources: commercial grower listings (specialty tropical plant retailers)
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Maranta species notes

planting.note: Plant divisions in moist, peat-based, well-drained soil in bright indirect shade; this uncommon prayer plant species needs consistently high humidity and warmth above 60°F to perform well.

directions: A less commonly offered relative of the familiar prayer plant, Maranta cristata produces thick, almost waxy, tuft-forming leaves in mint green marked with a lime-green central band and fine dark spotting, with purple-tinted undersides that show whenever the foliage folds upward at night. Like other Maranta species it exhibits true nyctinasty, with leaves lying flat during the day and lifting into a praying posture as light fades. Grow in consistently moist, peat-based soil in bright indirect shade, and maintain high humidity, since this species is less forgiving of dry indoor air than the common prayer plant. Propagate by dividing the rhizome, keeping several growth points per division.
sources: commercial grower listings (specialty tropical plant retailers)
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Maranta species notes
